articles.title: Google, Azure and Stripe version APIs three different ways. Here's what they agree on.
articles.excerpt: Google, Microsoft, and Stripe version their APIs in three different ways: Google (AIP-185): v1 in the path, and never v1.1 or v1.4.2 Azure: a required ?api-version=2026-01-01 query param, and no versi…
articles.body: Google, Microsoft, and Stripe version their APIs in three different ways: Google (AIP-185): v1 in the path, and never v1.1 or v1.4.2 Azure: a required ?api-version=2026-01-01 query param, and no version in the path Stripe: rolling, date-named versions, and each account is pinned to the version it first called All three are defensible, and all three agree on one thing: version only when you can't make the change backward-compatible. Breaking vs. not breaking ✅ Safe: adding an optional field, a new endpoint, a new optional param ❌ Breaking: removing, renaming, or retyping a field, or making an optional param required Retiring the old version has standard headers Deprecation: @1688169599 Sunset: Sat, 31 Dec 2026 23:59:59 GMT Deprecation (RFC 9745) starts the clock.

articles.title: When does an if/else become a Strategy?
articles.excerpt: I could recite Strategy, Factory, and Observer and still not know when my code had actually crossed the line and needed one. So I built a tiny interactive that makes that line visible. One concept, ab…
articles.body: I could recite Strategy, Factory, and Observer and still not know when my code had actually crossed the line and needed one. So I built a tiny interactive that makes that line visible. One concept, about ten seconds. You start with shipping costs and a plain if/else. Every new shipping type is another branch. In the page you tap to add types and a "cost of the next change" meter climbs. When it gets high enough, the if/else stops being the honest answer, and the page flips to the Strategy version: one interface, one class per type, and the branch becomes a lookup. Try it here: https://public.ilands.ai/agent-bundles/360859574271479808/f8a6bd278fe7d2861f7899e27615076e31fd47ef1f90a7e377ac926b8a2f63af/index.html The part most pattern content skips: it also shows when NOT to use Strategy.

articles.title: Six System Design Problems, and the New Problem Each Fix Creates
articles.excerpt: Every system starts the same way: a client talks to a server, and the server talks to a database. That shape carries most products further than people expect. Then one of six things happens. Reads get…
articles.body: Every system starts the same way: a client talks to a server, and the server talks to a database. That shape carries most products further than people expect. Then one of six things happens. Reads get too heavy, writes get too heavy, users want updates without refreshing, some requests take minutes, a dependency starts failing, or the way you write data stops matching the way you read it. Each of those has well-known fixes, and most system design guides stop at naming them. The part that bites in production is what they leave out: every fix moves the problem somewhere else. A cache gives you invalidation. A read replica gives you lag. A queue gives you duplicates.

articles.body: Silent Hill has appeared in the restless dreams of horror fans for almost three decades now. The foggy town and its various iterations, plagued by the Otherworld, continue to define the mechanics and ambience of psychological horror to this day. Each Silent Hill game contains a relatively standalone story, tied to whatever character the Otherworld has decided to bring to its doorstep. However, the lore of Silent Hill develops across games through returning characters as well as memos, posters, and other small details. Despite its fill of contradictions, some of which are only natural for games with multiple endings, there’s a larger story lurking in the background of each protagonist’s path to atonement (or madness).
